title: Surge mix benchmark notes — Amber scan
content:
Summary

This is a working note for the 'Amber' surge-mix sweep — a lightweight exploratory benchmark to understand how mixed request populations (interactive microbursts + background embedding jobs + occasional long-chat sessions) impact p50/p95/p99 latency and dollars-per-1k-queries across three serving configurations. Goal: produce a small set of heuristics we can operationalize in Optimize and Console (prefetch thresholds, SLO tiering, routing hints).

Key hypotheses (what we're testing)
- H1: Small, frequent microbursts (5–20 qps for <10s) cause disproportionate p99 degradation on smallbatch configs versus multiplexing/slotization.
- H2: Mixed workloads amplify cold-start cost if prewarm thresholds are conservative; quantify dollars/1k delta.
- H3: Predictable background embedding load can be shifted to compact quantized instances with minimal p50 impact for interactive traffic if routing prioritizes short tails.

Experiment matrix (quick)
- Workload mixes (3):
  A) 85% short chat-turns (avg tokens 40), 10% microburst spikes (2–20 requests in <6s), 5% embeddings (batch dim 128)
  B) 60% short chat, 30% sustained medium sessions (avg tokens 300), 10% embeddings
  C) 50% microburst-heavy (many 1–3 turn sessions), 40% embeddings, 10% long chat
- Configs (3):
  1) Hosted-highperf: autoscale aggressive, fast prewarm, default batching (small batch), 80ms baseline kernel latency
  2) Dedicated-compact: reserved tiles, quantized kernels (4-bit), slotized multiplexing, slower single-request p50 but cheaper token cost
  3) Private-quantized: on-prem with hybrid prefetch, pre-warmed KV caches, highest cold penalty but best isolation
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 (ms), tail jitter (p99-p95), throughput (QPS sustained), dollars per 1k queries (approx using cost model), CPU/GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate for sessions

Raw ASCII charts (selected snapshots)
- Workload A, 1k-query normalized costs and latencies (single run snapshot):

Table: config | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | $/1k
Hosted-highperf | 62 | 210 | 920 | $3.8
Dedicated-compact | 95 | 360 | 1300 | $2.1
Private-quantized | 110 | 420 | 1600 | $1.7

Observation: hosted gives best p50 and p95 for A but p99 suffers during microbursts due to prewarm thrash — we saw occasional 2–3s outliers at minute boundaries. Dedicated-compact reduces $/1k by ~45% but p99 is ~40% worse than hosted. Private is cheapest but p99 and burst penalty highest.

- Workload C (microburst-heavy), focused tail behavior:

Sketch (p99 time-series, ascii sparkline per config over a 10-minute run):
Hosted-highperf: ▂▁▂▇▇▇▇▇▂▁▁▇  (spikes at microbursts, amplitude up to 2.3s)
Dedicated-compact: ▂▂▂▂▇▇▇▇▇▇▇  (more sustained high tail during contiguous microbursts)
Private-quantized: ▂▁▁▁▁▇▇▇▇▇▇▇  (cold penalties when prewarm not triggered)

- Dollars sensitivity table (approx, Workload A–C averaged):

Table: config | avg $/1k (A) | avg $/1k (B) | avg $/1k (C)
Hosted-highperf | $3.8 | $4.5 | $5.1
Dedicated-compact | $2.1 | $2.3 | $2.7
Private-quantized | $1.7 | $1.9 | $2.2

Notes: the hosted cost rises with sustained sessions because autoscale introduces per-minute allocation costs; dedicated remains relatively flat due to reserved capacity amortization. Private has a higher cold-start capital penalty on bursty patterns.

Small qualitative traces (why p99 diverges)
- Prewarm policy mismatch: hosted uses a conservative warm-window (30s sustained) and frequently scales down between microbursts; the next spike re-triggers instance creation and kernel warm which shows as multi-second tails.
- Multiplexing vs small-batch trade: dedicated-compact keeps many slots and multiplexes but when spike cardinality saturates slots, queued requests grow linearly causing elevated p99.
- KV cache warm: long sessions benefit from high KV hit; lots of short sessions reduce hit rate and increase decode work.

Preliminary heuristics (actionable)
- For mixed traffic with >20% microburst probability, recommend: increase hosted prewarm aggressiveness for p99-sensitive routes OR route microburst-prone clients to dedicated pools with tiled multiplexing.
- For customers prioritizing units/economics, recommend devoted compact pools with routing hints: mark large embedding batches for compact pool; flag interactive sessions for low-latency pool.
- In Console: show an inline "burst-risk" indicator (estimated p99 delta if route is run on compact vs hosted) computed from recent session histograms.

Open questions / TODOs
- Run the same matrix but with model quant-profiles toggled (int8 vs 4-bit) to see whether the p99 delta compresses for compact pools. (Jira ENG-4999)
- Repeat experiments with higher concurrency per node (2x) to check slot contention vs tiling tradeoffs.
- Need more runs to compute statistical confidence intervals for p99 (we only did 3 seeds per cell).

Quick reproducibility notes
- harness: benchmarks/surge-mix/amber-scan (see linked PR).
- synthetic client: client/surge-generator v0.9 — uses poisson arrival for short sessions, periodic embedding bursts (20s), and long sessions sampled from production percentiles.
- cost model: approximate token-level cost + infra amortization; exact script at /infra/cost-scripts/amber-econ.py (linked PR).

Slack threads and references
- #optimize-bench (thread: "amber-scan initial") — contains raw CSVs and trace links.
- Confluence: OPT-amber-scan (dashboard snapshots + plots).

Closing thoughts (working)
This run confirms the canonical trade-off we expect: unit economics vs tail-latency. The interesting bit: mixed workloads with small high-frequency microbursts give hosting providers (with fast prewarm) short p95 wins but leave a stubborn long tail unless prewarm thresholds are tuned. Dedicated compact pools are materially cheaper and predictable but require careful routing & slot provisioning to avoid sustained p99 increases.

Next immediate steps
- Add quantized kernel sweep and re-run cell (1) and (3). Owner: Priya (by 2029-06-26).
- Draft Console UX copy for "burst-risk" indicator and add a simple estimate chart to Console mock (owner: Zoe).
- Create an internal playbook for customers: "When to pick Dedicated-compact vs Hosted-highperf" — first draft by Liam.

Notes to self: keep these writeups raw — they'll go into a more formal Optimize playbook if the heuristics hold.

End of note.
